Saha in the Atharvaveda is, according to Roth, the name of a plant, but Bloomfield thinks the word is only an adjective meaning ‘mighty.’
Foot notes xi. 6, 15. Cf. Sāmavidhāna brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 10.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v. 2b.
Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 648.
Cf. Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 642; Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 72.

Saha-deva is the name of a prince in the Rigveda, where he is victorious over the Śimyus and Dasyus. It is quite probable that he is identical with King sahadeva sārñjaya, who is mentioned in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa as having once been called suplan sārñjaya, and as having changed his name because of his success in performing the dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice. In the aitareya brāhmaṇa he is mentioned with Somaka Sahadevya, who also appears in the Rigveda.

Saha-devī is the name of a plant in the Atharvaveda according to the reading of the commentary.
Foot notes vi. 59, 2. Cf. Grill, Hundert Lieder,^2 163; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 325; Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 490, who does not accept this reading. A plant called sahadeva occurs in the Sāmavidhāna brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 10.
Sahamāna is the name of a plant in the Atharvaveda (ii. 25, 2; iv. 17, 2; viii. 2, 6; 7, 5).
